statement: The gradient of a differentiable scalar function f(x1,...,xn) is the unique vector field ∇f such that, at each point x, its dot product with any unit vector v̂ equals the directional derivative of f along v̂: (∇f(x))·v̂ = D_v f(x). In Cartesian coordinates with the Euclidean metric, ∇f = (∂f/∂x1, ..., ∂f/∂xn), conventionally written as a column vector.

symbols.meaning: scalar-valued differentiable function of n variables
directional derivative of f along v̂ at x
total derivative (differential) of f at x, dual to the gradient

properties.property: Defining property: ∇f is the unique vector field satisfying (∇f(x))·v̂ = D_v f(x) for every unit vector v̂ at each point x.
properties.why: this is how the gradient is defined, independent of coordinate system

properties.property: In Cartesian coordinates, ∇f(x,y,z) = (∂f/∂x) i + (∂f/∂y) j + (∂f/∂z) k, i.e. the column vector of partial derivatives.
properties.why: explicit component formula for the standard Euclidean case

properties.property: The gradient ∇f and the total derivative (differential) df are transpose of each other: ∇f is a column vector, df is the row vector with the same components; (df_x)(v) = ∇f(x)·v.
properties.why: the gradient is dual to the derivative under the Euclidean metric identification of tangent and cotangent spaces

properties.property: Fréchet-derivative characterization: ∇f(x) is the vector satisfying lim_{h→0} |f(x+h) − f(x) − ∇f(x)·h| / ‖h‖ = 0.
properties.why: equivalent analytic definition of differentiability and the gradient

properties.property: Linear approximation: f(x) ≈ f(x0) + (∇f)_{x0}·(x − x0) for x near x0.
properties.why: the gradient gives the best linear (first-order Taylor) approximation of f
follows directly from linearity of the partial derivative / directional derivative
standard product rule applied componentwise to the gradient

properties.property: Chain rule (curve form): (f∘g)'(c) = ∇f(a)·g'(c) for a parametric curve g with g(c)=a. General form: ∇(f∘g)(c) = (Dg(c))^T (∇f(a)) for g: R^k → R^n. Scalar-outer form: ∇(h∘f)(a) = h'(f(a)) ∇f(a).
properties.why: composition rules needed to propagate gradients through composite functions

properties.property: In non-Cartesian orthogonal coordinates (e.g. cylindrical, spherical) or general coordinates, the simple partial-derivative formula does not hold directly; the correct expression requires scale factors h_i or the inverse metric tensor g^{ij}: ∇f = Σ_i (1/h_i) (∂f/∂x^i) ê_i, or ∇f = (∂f/∂x^i) g^{ij} e_j in general coordinates.
properties.why: the Cartesian component formula is specific to an orthonormal Euclidean basis; other coordinate systems require metric correction factors

assumptions.assumption: f is differentiable at the point(s) in question.
assumptions.breaks_when: f is not differentiable there, e.g. has a kink or discontinuity — the gradient does not exist even if partial derivatives exist along some directions

assumptions.assumption: The Cartesian component formula ∇f = (∂f/∂x1,...,∂f/∂xn) assumes a Euclidean metric with an orthonormal basis.
assumptions.breaks_when: working in curvilinear or non-orthogonal coordinates, where the metric tensor / scale factors must be included

failure_modes.signature: directional derivatives exist but are not linear in the direction, or partial derivatives are discontinuous / undefined at a point
failure_modes.cause: f is not differentiable at that point, only partially or directionally differentiable

failure_modes.mode: Using the plain partial-derivative vector as the gradient in curvilinear coordinates
failure_modes.signature: computed vector has wrong magnitude or direction compared to the true gradient
failure_modes.cause: omitting the metric tensor g^{ij} or scale factors h_i required outside Cartesian/Euclidean orthonormal coordinates
